PRD.when: When you have a category in mind but no product, and want one run from buyer complaints to a scored pick.
PRD.tune: Feed it reviews from Amazon and from three to five rival Shopify stores, plus a real landed cost from a supplier quote so the last step can score margin. Do not jump straight to the score: the gap step should change one thing buyers notice, not three. Read PRD-0001, PRD-0002 and PRD-0006 before you start.

PRD.when: When you want to open a store or add a line and have a market in mind but no product yet.
PRD.tune: Favour problems people pay to fix again and again, and drop any that only support a cheap one-off item. Check who already advertises to each problem in the Meta Ad Library for your selling country before you shortlist. Read PRD-0012 and PRD-0013 first so the top five lean toward repeat buys and parcel-friendly goods.

PRD.when: When you want proof of unmet demand in a category before you design or source anything.
PRD.tune: Paste one- to three-star reviews from Amazon and the top Shopify rivals, sorted by star, and keep the review lines next to each pain. A badly rated subcategory with weak search volume is a trap, so confirm search demand before you call it a gap. Check PRD-0002 so the fix is one clear change, and AVT-0009 for buyers who already spent money on failed fixes.

PRD.when: When your category looks the same everywhere and you need the one difference that would make buyers switch.
PRD.tune: Give it prices, pack shots, claims and review counts for three to five leaders, plus any shift in taste you see among your buyers. Pick one change only, since a new format, price and claim at once confuses shoppers. Read PRD-0001 and PRD-0002 first, then BRD-0011 to turn the gap into a position.

PRD.when: When you want products other stores already sell with ads and you have no paid spy tool.
PRD.tune: Use the free Meta Ad Library set to your selling country, and log how long each ad has run and how many stores run it. A viral video with no ads behind it is not proof, and one-hit products fade fast, so read PRD-0003 before you order stock. Pass the shortlist to the saturation and scoring checks next.

PRD.when: When you have one to three product ideas and want a go or no-go before you spend on stock or ads.
PRD.tune: Feed it the landed cost from a real supplier quote, the price rivals charge, parcel size and weight, and whether buyers reorder. A product that can only sell cheap rarely funds paid ads, so check PRD-0006 first and PRD-0013 for repeat and gifting demand. Use your real shipping rates for India or the US, not the supplier's estimate.

PRD.when: When a product looks promising and you need to know how many stores already run ads for it.
PRD.tune: Run it in the Meta Ad Library for each country you plan to sell in and date the result, since counts change week to week. It misses Amazon and TikTok Shop sellers, so check those by hand. A crowded field can still be won with a better offer, so read PRD-0002 and OFF-0035 before you drop the idea.

PRD.when: When a product or category is trending and you need to know if it is a fad before you buy stock.
PRD.tune: Give it five years of Google Trends data, not one, plus the selling season in your country. If your store already rides one hot product, use the range question to plan what comes next. Read PRD-0003 on how hero products decay and PRD-0001 on picking big, known categories.

PRD.when: When you found a rival store selling your product and want to know if the market is big enough to chase.
PRD.tune: Use visit estimates from a traffic tool and the rival's real price and bundle mix from their store, then read the result as a range, not one number. A store with heavy paid traffic can show big sales and little profit. Check PRD-0017 on how channels split and PRD-0006 before you size your own plan.

PRD.when: When you already sell and must choose your next product with more ideas than cash.
PRD.tune: Feed it your Shopify order export, repeat rate by product and ad results for any test of the new item. A launch that sells to your own email list but not to cold traffic has not proven it can win new customers, so read PRD-0012 first. PRD-0011 warns against splitting cash before the hero product is fully backed.

PRD.when: When your range has grown and shoppers or ads no longer say clearly what you sell.
PRD.tune: List every SKU with sales, margin and the job it does for the buyer, using your Shopify product sales report. Do not add a SKU only because a rival has one. Read PRD-0011 on backing one hero and PRD-0007 on line extensions before you approve a launch.

PRD.when: When you want to sell a new kind of product under your current store name.
PRD.tune: Give it what your brand means today, in buyers' words from reviews, and the new product. Do not stretch the name just to save on ads, because the new line can blur what the core product stands for. Read PRD-0008 and PRD-0007 first, and BRD-0012 if a new name is needed.

PRD.when: When you want a steady monthly routine for finding and screening your next product, not a one-off hunch.
PRD.tune: Each month give it saved Ad Library captures, marketplace best-seller ranks and your cost notes, since it cannot browse. Keep a watch list so a product that has filled up with rivals is dropped before you order. Read PRD-0003 and PRD-0012 so its picks favour products that win new buyers and last.

PRD.when: When you want to test real demand with a pre-order or waitlist page before you place a factory order.
PRD.tune: Set the pass mark in paid pre-orders or deposits, not email sign-ups, and send a small Meta test to a Shopify pre-order page. State the ship date and refund terms plainly, since late pre-orders hurt trust and can breach payment provider rules. Check PRD-0006 so the test price matches the price you plan to sell at.

PRD.when: When you are turning an everyday annoyance into a product on a small budget and want to think it through.
PRD.tune: Bring the problem, who else has it and your cash limit, and ask where to pay experts and where to do it yourself. Her record is about one hero product and getting it seen, so pair it with PRD-0011 and PRD-0003 on hero focus and decay.

AVT.when: When your ads or product page sound generic and you cannot say who the buyer is in one breath.
AVT.tune: Search Reddit and niche forums in the buyer's own problem words, plus your reviews and rivals', and paste exact quotes rather than summaries. Keep to the 60-minute box so research does not stall the launch. Read AVT-0006, AVT-0007 and AVT-0011 first.

AVT.when: When you want to know what rival products leave out and which promises buyers no longer believe.
AVT.tune: Paste Amazon and rival-store reviews split by star, and pull out the one- and five-star reviews that mention money spent on other fixes. With fewer than about 100 reviews, treat each point as a lead, not a pattern. Read AVT-0009, AVT-0008 and AVT-0010 first.

AVT.when: When you have reviews and survey answers but do not know which kinds of buyer they come from.
AVT.tune: Feed it your review app export, post-purchase survey answers and rival reviews, and count self-describing phrases such as "as a nurse". A group that shows up once is not a segment. Read AVT-0016 and AVT-0013 first.

AVT.when: When you sell a product many stores sell and bigger rivals own the obvious buyer.
AVT.tune: Give it rival ads from the Meta Ad Library and long Amazon reviews with photos or video, then size each new group with a Reddit search. If your product is the same as the leader's, a new buyer group is the cheaper win than a new mechanism. Read AVT-0014, AVT-0012 and AVT-0013 first.

AVT.when: When your avatar is a list of ages and incomes and your ads still miss.
AVT.tune: Feed it buyer stories, support tickets from your helpdesk and survey answers, so each card ties a job and a trigger to a real quote. Watch for odd uses of your product, which can be separate jobs and even new SKUs. Read AVT-0003 and AVT-0005 first.

AVT.when: When your reviews are short and you want to call five to eight recent buyers to learn why they bought.
AVT.tune: Paste the Shopify orders for each buyer you will call, with first product, discount code and days to reorder, so each call starts from facts. Ask about the timeline from first thought to purchase, never which features to add. Read AVT-0003, then AVT-0017 and AVT-0024 for how many calls are enough.

AVT.when: When you have a customer list and want to hear from buyers and non-buyers before you pick angles, offers or the next product.
AVT.tune: Pull buyers and non-buying subscribers from Klaviyo and promise no sales pitch in the invite. Use a reward everyone gets plus a prize draw, and check your local rules on draws in India or the US. Read AVT-0018, AVT-0025 and AVT-0021 first.

AVT.when: When you get orders but cannot say why people bought or what nearly stopped them.
AVT.tune: Run the survey on the Shopify thank-you page and as a Klaviyo email, and ask what they tried before your product. When you read results, weight the most loyal and the least happy buyers over the middle. Read AVT-0021 and AVT-0019 first.

AVT.when: When your product quiz has about 100 answers and you have not read them as a whole.
AVT.tune: Export quiz answers from your quiz app or Klaviyo profile fields about every 100 submissions. The share of people naming failed past fixes shows how aware they are, so read that before picking a hook. Read AVT-0023, AVT-0022 and AVT-0020 first.

AVT.when: When ads show strong returns but repeat orders and profit stay weak, and you want to know who your best buyers really are.
AVT.tune: Feed it the Shopify customer and order export with discount codes, first product and UTM source. Sale-only buyers often never come back, so do not let them shape your avatar. Read AVT-0021 and OFF-0008 first.

AVT.when: When you are about to test a new buyer group and want the ad, page and photos to speak to the same person.
AVT.tune: Paste the buyer sketch with its quotes, the ad, and the product page text and images. Adding the group's name to the hook alone fails, so every part must match. Read AVT-0015 and AVT-0012 first.

AVT.when: When a poll or survey says people love an idea and you are about to launch, rename or reprice because of it.
AVT.tune: Paste the questions, answers and sample size, then compare them with what buyers actually did in Shopify. Stated love rarely matches orders, so turn the answer into a pre-order or click test before you act. Read AVT-0019 first.

AVT.when: When you have notes from buyer interviews and no clear pattern for why people switched to you.
AVT.tune: Use notes from calls with recent buyers, not reviews, and mark what pushed them off the old fix and what nearly held them back. These forces become ad and page angles, so keep the exact quotes. Read AVT-0003 and AVT-0009 first.

AVT.when: When new reviews arrive every month and you want your buyer file kept current without reading each one.
AVT.tune: Give it each month's review export from your store, Amazon and your review app, along with your brand file. When low reviews rise, it should split product faults from wrong-fit buyers, since they need different fixes. Read AVT-0016 and AVT-0008 first.

AVT.when: When you want to think through the real job a buyer hires your product to do.
AVT.tune: Bring buyer stories and the odd ways people use your product, and ask about situations and struggles rather than age and income. Pair it with AVT-0003 for the interview method and AVT-0005 for jobs that can become new SKUs.

OFF.when: When you want a better offer and do not know whether to change price, add a bundle, a gift or a subscription.
OFF.tune: Feed it gross margin per SKU, the spread of order values and repeat rate from your Shopify export. Try the free wins such as order bumps and gifts before levers that cost margin. Read OFF-0035, OFF-0014 and OFF-0015 first.

OFF.when: When you plan a sitewide sale, a code or free shipping and want to know the ad return it needs before it goes live.
OFF.tune: Use real cost of goods, shipping, payment and app fees per order, not list margin. The return you need climbs fast as a discount eats margin, so run every discount depth you are weighing. Read OFF-0005, OFF-0065, OFF-0069 and OFF-0033 first.

OFF.when: When you sell one hero product at one price and want a bigger first order.
OFF.tune: Give it unit cost, shipping cost per pack size and your current order mix from Shopify. Tie each tier to a real use, make the middle pack the default and space the savings evenly between tiers. Read OFF-0027, OFF-0049, OFF-0018 and OFF-0030 first.

OFF.when: When you want to set or fix a free-shipping or gift threshold without guessing from average order value.
OFF.tune: Export a year of order values from Shopify and set thresholds from the peaks, not the mean. Free shipping on a single cheap item can lose money, so test a multipack line instead. Read OFF-0013, OFF-0079, OFF-0076 and OFF-0033 first.

OFF.when: When you want cart and checkout add-ons that raise profit, not only order value.
OFF.tune: Give it products bought together and margin per SKU from Shopify, plus take rates from your upsell app if you have them. Rank each slot by take rate times added value times margin, and keep discounts out of checkout. Read OFF-0011, OFF-0009, OFF-0050 and OFF-0010 first.

OFF.when: When you are adding an after-payment offer and want to set what buyers see first and what follows a no.
OFF.tune: Use your post-purchase app results and margin per offer, and judge each slot by profit added per order, not take rate. The best offers are more of the same at a multi-unit price, or a product that fixes the next problem. Read OFF-0051, OFF-0052 and OFF-0074 first.

OFF.when: When you want a bigger order or a cheaper first sale without cutting your price.
OFF.tune: List low-cost items buyers want, with their landed cost and spare stock. A gift pays only when it lowers the cost to win a buyer by more than the gift costs, so recheck break-even with the gift included. Read OFF-0007, OFF-0073 and OFF-0078 first.

OFF.when: When you sell something people use up and want a subscription offer that wins first-order subscribers.
OFF.tune: Feed it margin, how long one unit lasts, repeat data by cohort and cash on hand. Front-load the first-order discount, give one-time buyers none, and match the delivery cadence to real use to cut cancels. Read OFF-0029, OFF-0040, OFF-0041 and OFF-0075 first.

OFF.when: When shoppers hesitate at checkout and you want to know if a stronger guarantee would pay.
OFF.tune: Give it monthly sales, refund rate by product and return shipping cost from Shopify. Work out net sales after the extra refunds before you lengthen the window, and offer lifetime cover only on goods that truly last. Read OFF-0001, OFF-0060, OFF-0064 and OFF-0056 first.

OFF.when: When your pop-up has offered the same small discount for months and few sign-ups turn into orders.
OFF.tune: Give it Klaviyo sign-up and placed-order rates, average order value and any live site offers. A one-time discount in the pop-up can undercut your subscription offer, and money-off framing often beats percent off on bigger orders. Read OFF-0026, OFF-0028, OFF-0036 and OFF-0037 first.

OFF.when: When you are planning Black Friday or a big seasonal sale and want backup offers ready before it starts.
OFF.tune: Feed it stock by SKU, margin and active subscriber count. Build the ladder of gift, bundle and deeper discount ahead of time, and give subscribers a better members-only deal so the sale does not trigger cancels. Read OFF-0068, OFF-0066, OFF-0043 and OFF-0008 first.

OFF.when: When you want a limited drop or a sale deadline that makes people act without fake timers.
OFF.tune: Use real stock counts and a real end date, and give your email list early access. Fake or always-on scarcity breaks trust and can break consumer rules in the US and India. Read OFF-0003 and OFF-0080 first.

OFF.when: When you tested two or more offers and need to know which one earns more per visitor.
OFF.tune: Paste sessions, orders, revenue and unit costs per variant from your test tool and Shopify. A higher order value can hide lower profit, so pick by profit per session and recheck break-even for each offer. Read OFF-0015 and OFF-0016 first.

OFF.when: When you set prices by feel and want one safe price test with a floor you will not cross.
OFF.tune: Give it unit costs, recent sales at each price and rival prices, and change the live price in Shopify yourself. Do not cut price on reflex when a rival does, but do test a lower price when a launch stalls, as OFF-0070 shows. Read OFF-0070 and FIN-0012 first.

OFF.when: When your offer feels plain and you want to work out what would make it hard to refuse.
OFF.tune: Bring the core product, buyer doubts from reviews and your margin, and push for bonuses and a guarantee rather than a lower price. Check any guarantee against your refund maths before you publish it. Read OFF-0002 and OFF-0001 first.

BRD.when: When your products look like everyone else's and you need a spot your rivals do not hold.
BRD.tune: Plot three to six real rivals using the prices, claims and looks on their stores and ads, then pick one corner. Look for an open place in the buyer's mind, not a gap in your own range. Read BRD-0011, BRD-0013 and BRD-0008 first.

BRD.when: When your home page tries to talk to everyone and you need one clear line on who the store is for.
BRD.tune: Give it your best customers' words from reviews and survey answers, plus the product. Write the not-for-you list too, since a promise that fits everyone fits no one. Read BRD-0011 and BRD-0001 first.

BRD.when: When you want to raise prices or stop leaning on sales and need a reason buyers will accept.
BRD.tune: Bring your buyer groups, review quotes and the real product reason you can charge more. A premium place has to be claimed first and backed up, and discount-heavy ads will undo it. Read BRD-0009 and BRD-0013 first.

BRD.when: When an AI is about to write or design anything for a store that already has a website.
BRD.tune: Point it at your live Shopify store so prices, offers, look and voice each carry a source, and rerun it after any price or offer change. Never let it adopt a rival's look as your own. Read BRD-0005 and BRD-0015 first.

BRD.when: When you are about to make Meta ads with the meta-ads skills and need a brand profile they can read.
BRD.tune: Run it on your store URL, then check its colours, fonts and voice against your main brand file before meta-create or meta-generate use it. It reads the site as it is today, so remove stale sale banners first. Read BRD-0005 and BRD-0015 first.

BRD.when: When you are opening a store or a new line and need a wide pool of names that fit your market.
BRD.tune: Give it the one feeling the name must carry, your rivals' names and every market you sell in, including a Hindi or regional sense check for India. Expect the best name to split the team, not please everyone. Read BRD-0002, BRD-0016, BRD-0018 and BRD-0012 first.

BRD.when: When you have two to five names and must pick one before you buy the domain or packaging.
BRD.tune: Paste the shortlist with your category and where you sell. Avoid initials-only names, score sound and spelling, and run your own trademark search in India and the US, since the tool cannot clear a name. Read BRD-0010, BRD-0017 and BRD-0019 first.

BRD.when: When you need one line for your header, pack and ads, or must choose between a few.
BRD.tune: Paste the tagline with your promise and key messages. An obvious line is rarely a good one, so push for one that is true but not expected. Read BRD-0021 and BRD-0011 first.

BRD.when: When you add a new range and cannot decide between a new name and your store name.
BRD.tune: List each range with its price level, buyers and sales. Put a product under the house name only when it fits the rules in PRD-0008, and run the shopping-list test in PRD-0007. Read BRD-0012 if a new name is needed.

BRD.when: When you doubt your store name, got a trademark letter, or are changing what the store stands for.
BRD.tune: Feed it branded search clicks from Search Console, direct traffic and repeat sales so the keep-or-rename score uses real numbers. Plan redirects and a clear story of why and what buyers gain. Read BRD-0020 and BRD-0010 first.

BRD.when: When your photos, pack and site look like they came from different brands and you need one look.
BRD.tune: Bring your positioning, three rival stores and images from far outside your category. Pick one colour, shape or scene you can own that works even without the logo. Read BRD-0003 and BRD-0005 first.

BRD.when: When you are redoing your box, tissue or insert and want every part to feel like one brand.
BRD.tune: Give it the product, the pack parts and the cost you can add per order. Match scent or sound to the visual mood, and get a safety check before adding scent near food, skincare or pet goods. Read BRD-0004 and BRD-0007 first.

BRD.when: When your site, emails and pack were made at different times and you suspect they no longer match.
BRD.tune: Attach screenshots of the home and product pages, a Klaviyo email, the pack and two live ads. Check that price signals back your position, above all before you move upmarket. Read BRD-0015, BRD-0009 and BRD-0005 first.

BRD.when: When several people or tools write your copy and you want each draft checked against your voice before it ships.
BRD.tune: Give it your brand file and voice rules, then each ad, email or product page draft. It should fix tone and leave claims as written, and log repeat mistakes so the brief gets better. Read BRD-0021 and BRD-0011 first.

BRD.when: When you want to think through which one word your brand should own, or whether to lead a new category.
BRD.tune: Bring your category, the leader and your range, and ask whether to narrow your focus or start a new category. Pair it with BRD-0013 on being first in the mind, BRD-0008 on why better copies fail and BRD-0014 on naming an imitation openly.

SET.when: When you are opening a new Shopify store and want every setup step done in the right order, up to a first test order.
SET.tune: Feed it your country, your legal business name, a product list export and carrier quotes, so each step builds on real data. Do not let it skip the closing test-order step, because most launch faults only show on a phone checkout. Read SET-0003 and SET-0005 before you start.

SET.when: When you have not opened your Shopify account yet and need to choose a plan, payments and domain first.
SET.tune: Give it the country the business is registered in and the currency you plan to charge, since Shopify Payments decides whether local prices carry through checkout. Enter legal names exactly as on government ID, as a nickname can stall payout checks. Cards SET-0005 and SET-0002 first.

SET.when: When you need to choose a theme or are thinking of moving away from the one you have.
SET.tune: List must-haves from your real catalogue: number of variants, a bundle picker, a mobile gallery and filters. Judge each demo on a phone with no apps added, because every app you add later slows it. Read SPD-0001 and LPG-0034.

SET.when: When you are about to add products and need sizes, colours and packs set up so nothing breaks later.
SET.tune: Start from the supplier sheet with unit cost, packed weight and box size for each variant, since shipping and margin reports read these fields. Enter packed weight, not the bare item weight. Check SET-0007 and MEA-0023.

SET.when: When your products need collections, filters and a menu so shoppers can find things fast.
SET.tune: Give it your product export with tags and your top search terms from Shopify search or Search Console. Name collections after what people search, not internal codes, so the same pages can rank later. Read SEO-0003 and LPG-0039.

SET.when: When you are setting shipping zones and rates, or shipping seems to be losing you money.
SET.tune: Feed it label costs by zone and the spread of order values from a Shopify orders export. Save every box as a package with its empty weight, or calculated rates will undercharge on every order. Check SET-0007 and LPG-0063.

SET.when: When you are setting up tax for a new store or starting to sell in a new state or country.
SET.tune: Tell it where you have an office, staff or stock, and which markets expect prices with tax included. Run a test cart to each state you ship to and confirm the shipping line is taxed the way that state wants. Read SET-0004 and leave registration questions to an accountant.

SET.when: When you want to sell to shoppers in other countries from one Shopify store.
SET.tune: Name your payment gateway first: without Shopify Payments, local prices stop at the cart and checkout charges your base currency. Test one checkout from each market before you spend on ads there. Read SET-0002 and SET-0009.

SET.when: When you are switching on payments or think a checkout setting is costing you orders.
SET.tune: Paste your payment provider, wallet and checkout settings plus the account verification status. Turn on Shop Pay and the other wallets before any other mobile checkout change, and fix name mismatches before payouts freeze. Check SET-0008 and SET-0005.

SET.when: When your store is built and you are about to remove the password and go live.
SET.tune: Give it your settings plus the results of real test orders placed on a phone to two or three addresses. A clean desktop order proves little, since tax, shipping rate and warehouse app errors show up on mobile and on other addresses. Read SET-0003 first.

SET.when: When you have a long list of apps and want to know which to keep, swap or cut.
SET.tune: Paste your Apps list with what each one does and your PageSpeed mobile score. Look for overlap first, such as two review apps or two pop-up tools, because each one adds scripts. Read SPD-0001 and SPD-0009.

SET.when: When chargebacks are rising or you have never set rules for risky orders.
SET.tune: Give it monthly orders and chargebacks with their reasons from your payments dispute report. Below about a hundred orders a month, keep the platform defaults, because tight rules decline real buyers. Read SET-0005 for keeping the payment account healthy.

SET.when: When Shopify's built-in discounts or shipping options cannot do the rule you need.
SET.tune: Describe the rule with a worked cart, such as percentage off with a cap for large orders, or a gift at a spend level. It writes a Shopify Function, so have a developer test it on a copy before it goes live. Read SET-0001 and LPG-0072.

SET.when: When overseas orders are growing and you wonder if a local store or warehouse would pay off.
SET.tune: Give it orders, returns and shipping cost by country from a Shopify sales by country report. Compare the full cost of each order delivered, with payment fees and duties, not postage alone. Read SET-0009 and MEA-0037.

SET.when: When you are building your store on WooCommerce instead of Shopify.
SET.tune: Tell it your host, payment gateway and country, and who will handle updates and backups. Plan for speed from day one by keeping plugins off pages that have no cart. Read SPD-0014 and SET-0003.

MEA.when: When you are about to raise ad spend and are not sure your tracking counts each sale once.
MEA.tune: Give it your GA4 setup notes, Meta Events Manager screenshots, how you tag links and 30 days of Shopify orders by day. Fix setup before you read any ROAS, because a leftover test event code or a missing event_id makes every later number wrong. Read MEA-0005, MEA-0006 and MEA-0042.

MEA.when: When you just set up GA4 or your purchases do not show up there.
MEA.tune: Describe your property settings, data retention, internal traffic filter and where the purchase event comes from. Set retention to 14 months on day one, since the change does not reach back. Filter key event rate to purchases before you read conversion by channel.

MEA.when: When Meta shows fewer purchases than your store or you just added server-side tracking.
MEA.tune: Feed it Events Manager screenshots: match quality, deduplication and server versus browser counts for Purchase. Check that one event_id travels on both the pixel and the server event and that no test code is left in the live tag. Read MEA-0001 before you promise a big recovery from a gateway.

MEA.when: When you are not sure which Meta attribution setting to trust or report on.
MEA.tune: Give it Ads Manager exports with the attribution comparison columns next to Shopify new-customer orders for the same days. Report on 7-day click, because much of the view-through credit disappears when checked. Read MEA-0042, MEA-0025 and MEA-0007.

MEA.when: When you are launching Google Ads or Google shows a different purchase count than your store.
MEA.tune: Give it your Shopify plan, the Google app status and any Tag Manager setup. Keep one primary purchase action with real order value and enhanced conversions, since GA4-imported purchases undercount as the primary. Read MEA-0016 and MEA-0017.

MEA.when: When you make choices from the Shopify dashboard and want to know which tiles you can trust.
MEA.tune: Paste the analytics tiles with their date range and a sales report by day. Use net sales plus shipping as cash collected, and read returning customer rate as a share of orders, not a repeat rate. Read MEA-0010, MEA-0013 and MEA-0021.

MEA.when: When you need your true margin per order before you set any ad target.
MEA.tune: Give it price, unit cost, freight in, packaging, pick and pack, postage, payment fees and expected return rate for each product. Margin must be the cost to the customer's door, not the product margin Shopify shows from the cost field. This is the trust gate, so read MEA-0023 and MEA-0037 before ranking any play.

MEA.when: When you need break-even ROAS, a cost per customer ceiling or a budget forecast worked out from your numbers.
MEA.tune: Paste an Ads Manager export plus the delivered margin from the margin check, never revenue alone. Check the cost per customer floor from cost per click and conversion rate before you plan to scale. Read MEA-0019, MEA-0047 and MEA-0026.

MEA.when: When total revenue looks fine but you cannot tell what new customers are costing you.
MEA.tune: Feed it a Shopify orders export with the new or returning flag, product costs and daily spend from Meta and Google. Make new-customer MER the headline, not blended MER, because repeat buyers hide rising acquisition costs. Read MEA-0039, MEA-0025 and MEA-0031.

MEA.when: When you only find out at month end whether a day or a week made money.
MEA.tune: Give it daily net sales, variable costs, ad spend and your 90-day return rate. Accrue returns each day at the expected rate, because Shopify books them on the refund date, and keep fixed costs out of the daily view. Read MEA-0030, MEA-0028 and MEA-0011.

MEA.when: When you want to know if you can safely raise ad spend based on what customers are worth over time.
MEA.tune: Give it Shopify revenue by first-order month, gross margin, new customers and spend. Use 30-day or 90-day gross profit per customer, not lifetime revenue, and only judge cohorts old enough to fill that window. Read MEA-0020, MEA-0054 and MEA-0048.

MEA.when: When platform ROAS looks great but the bank balance does not agree.
MEA.tune: Put Meta and Google exports for the same dates next to Shopify net sales and new-customer revenue. Be wary of small channels and retargeting that look strong because they catch warm visitors. Read MEA-0053, MEA-0040 and, if you also sell on Amazon, MEA-0029.

MEA.when: When your ad reports and your customers' own answers about how they found you disagree.
MEA.tune: Give it the how-did-you-hear answers from your post-purchase survey app and spend by channel for the same weeks. Compare each channel's share of answers with its share of spend, and make sure AI assistants are one of the answer options. Read MEA-0045 and AEO-0025.

MEA.when: When a channel's reported sales and your store's sales do not match and you need to know what the ads really add.
MEA.tune: Give it spend, new-customer revenue and new orders by region for several months. Match test regions on all three histories and keep the test well clear of Black Friday. Read MEA-0050, MEA-0033 and MEA-0034, and MEA-0041 if the store is small.

MEA.when: When sales dropped and you want to know which lever moved before you change anything.
MEA.tune: Feed it Shopify sessions, orders and AOV for both periods, plus the ad change history and returns. Split the drop into sessions, conversion rate and order value, and remember that Google's last few days always look weak. Read MEA-0009, MEA-0018 and MEA-0051.

LPG.when: When Meta ads get clicks but the page they land on does not sell.
LPG.tune: Give it the live ad, the landing link, a phone screenshot and the Events Manager view for that page. Confirm the pixel records a page view after the cookie banner, then check message match and trust in the first screen. Read LPG-0064, LPG-0038 and MEA-0007.

LPG.when: When you are about to send paid traffic to a page and want to check it keeps the ad's promise.
LPG.tune: Attach the exact ad copy and first frame from any channel, with the page it links to. Each persona or angle ad should land on a page that leads with that one benefit. Read LPG-0064, LPG-0067 and LPG-0068.

LPG.when: When you run ads to several buyer groups and need to decide which page each one should land on.
LPG.tune: Give it your live ads tagged by buyer group, awareness stage and traffic source. Social traffic needs the pain and education block early, while search traffic wants product and price first. Read LPG-0070, LPG-0050 and LPG-0004.

LPG.when: When people land on your page but leave before scrolling, and you suspect the first screen.
LPG.tune: Give it your offer, review count and rating, guarantee terms and your best ad headlines. Test the headline first and the hero image second, and put returns or guarantee lines right under the button. Read LPG-0016, LPG-0067 and LPG-0038.

LPG.when: When you are building or fixing a product page that must answer the doubts that stop buyers.
LPG.tune: Feed it answers to 'what almost stopped you buying', support tickets and low-star reviews. Plan for phones first: thumbnails, rating above the title, and price, add to cart and risk reducers in the first screen. Read LPG-0034, LPG-0048 and LPG-0042.

LPG.when: When your page has reviews but visitors still leave before buying.
LPG.tune: Give it a review export with names and photos from your reviews app, plus your top buying objections. Choose each testimonial to answer one objection and show who wrote it, since bare logos and anonymous quotes now read as fake. Read LPG-0053, LPG-0037 and LPG-0062.

LPG.when: When your product page offers many pack sizes and most buyers still pick the smallest.
LPG.tune: Give it unit cost, shipping cost per pack and current pack choices from Shopify orders. Cut to three tiers, put the money saved in each option's title and check margin per tier before you test. Read LPG-0006, LPG-0008 and LPG-0035.

LPG.when: When your product photos are mostly pack shots and shoppers keep asking about size, use or fit.
LPG.tune: Give it the current gallery, the top questions from email and chat, and review quotes. More shoppers swipe the whole gallery than scroll the whole page, so let the images carry answers and proof. Read LPG-0060 and LPG-0034.

LPG.when: When you have an ad that works and want to know if a long article-style page is worth building.
LPG.tune: Give it results from the ad running to a plain product page: spend, cost per purchase against break-even and the angle used. Build an advertorial only once the plain page roughly breaks even, and match page length to how hard the ad already sells. Read LPG-0030, LPG-0029 and LPG-0004.

LPG.when: When the readiness check says go and you need a full advertorial written and checked for cold traffic.
LPG.tune: Ground it in customer research, a buyer sheet, an offer brief, a short belief list and real reviews. Keep one editorial voice from start to end and close with a soft check-availability step. Read LPG-0057, LPG-0044 and LPG-0025.

LPG.when: When your product needs matching to the buyer and ad traffic does not convert on a plain product page.
LPG.tune: Give it survey answers, review themes and which product suits which buyer. Treat the first three questions as the hook and test them first, and aim for about 30% of starters to reach the results page. Read LPG-0032, LPG-0019 and CRO-0004.

LPG.when: When your store has grown cluttered and shoppers reach product pages but few add to cart.
LPG.tune: Attach phone screenshots of home, collection, product and cart pages, plus click map data if you have it. Remove parts that get under about 1% of clicks, and hide the discount code box when no promotion is running. Read LPG-0043, LPG-0007 and LPG-0058.

LPG.when: When collection pages get visits but few clicks into products, often because popular sizes are sold out.
LPG.tune: Give it the product order of your top collection and stock by size from Shopify inventory. Paid visitors judge a collection by its top six products, so move broken-size items down every day. Read LPG-0069, LPG-0059 and LPG-0041.

LPG.when: When your menu is messy and your best products take too many taps to reach.
LPG.tune: Give it collections ranked by sales and menu clicks from your analytics. Put a bestsellers row at the top of the phone menu, use image categories and keep links that lead away from a product off product pages. Read LPG-0039, LPG-0061 and LPG-0071.

LPG.when: When your page copy is final and you need it turned into a Shopify page you can edit yourself.
LPG.tune: Paste the approved copy and name your theme so the sections read price from the product and never go stale. Install on a duplicate theme and check on a phone before publishing. Read LPG-0013 before adding a sticky buy button to a long page.

SPD.when: When your Shopify store is slow and you want fixes made in the order that wins back the most orders.
SPD.tune: Give it PageSpeed reports for the home page, top collection and top product page, your app list and theme files. Fix images first, then outside scripts, then hosting. Read SPD-0002, SPD-0001 and SPD-0004.

SPD.when: When your mobile speed score is low or Search Console warns about Core Web Vitals.
SPD.tune: Run PageSpeed Insights on a home, collection and product page and paste all three with the field data. Field data is a rolling 28-day sample of real visits, so judge a fix on lab data now and field data a month later. Read SPD-0005 and SPD-0006.

SPD.when: When a speed audit lists many problems and you need to know which ones are worth the time.
SPD.tune: Give it the problem list plus monthly sessions, conversion rate and order value from Shopify. Size each payoff from your own field data and published cases, never from a promised lift. Read SPD-0004 and SPD-0002.

SPD.when: When you have many apps and a slow mobile score and want to know which apps cost the most speed.
SPD.tune: Paste your Apps list and the third-party code section of the PageSpeed report. Stores with few outside services score far better on mobile, so cut duplicate apps before you tune the rest. Read SPD-0001 and SPD-0011.

SPD.when: When you removed an app but its script still shows up in PageSpeed.
SPD.tune: Give it the files from a duplicate theme and the name of every app you have removed. Search the theme for each app's name and delete lines on the copy first. Read SPD-0009.

SPD.when: When the first big image on your page appears late and LCP is above 2.5 seconds.
SPD.tune: Give it the hero or slider section code and the LCP element named in PageSpeed. Load the first hero image right away with high priority and never fade it in. Read SPD-0006 and SPD-0008.

SPD.when: When a bar, badge or image pushes the page down as it loads.
SPD.tune: Give it the layout shift report and the page, and name any app that adds a bar or badge. App-added free-shipping bars are a common cause, so use a theme block or reserve the space. Read SPD-0007.

SPD.when: When scripts, styles or fonts block your first screen from showing on phones.
SPD.tune: Give it theme.liquid, the apps you are keeping and your font setup. Most app code enters through the theme head, so delay only scripts you can find and leave checkout and tracking code alone. Read SPD-0011 and SPD-0009.

SPD.when: When you are about to upload product or banner images, or your image files are over 1 MB.
SPD.tune: List file names, sizes and pixel widths from Shopify Files. Shopify only lightly compresses uploads, so size images to about twice their shown width and compress before you upload. Read SPD-0008 and SPD-0013.

SPD.when: When your homepage has sliders, autoplay video or quick view, and pages feel slow.
SPD.tune: Give it home and collection page screenshots plus the theme settings for sliders, video and quick view. Swap video embeds for a light thumbnail and remove quick view that loads every product's data. Read SPD-0010 and SPD-0012.

SPD.when: When a big sale or ad push is coming and you want speed checked and protected beforehand.
SPD.tune: Give it the sale date, current scores and any apps or banners planned for the sale. Set a limit per page and test again after each new app or banner. Read SPD-0005, and SPD-0003 for cart and checkout caching rules.

SPD.when: When your store runs on WooCommerce or another self-hosted system and pages are slow.
SPD.tune: Give it your host, caching plugin, plugin list and server response time. Never cache cart, checkout or account pages, and stop WooCommerce files loading on pages with no cart. Read SPD-0014 and SPD-0003.

SPD.when: When you add apps often and want speed checked the same way every month.
SPD.tune: Give it each month's PageSpeed reports and app list so it can compare with the month before. Under about 1,000 sessions a month, run the single report reader instead. Read SPD-0005 and SPD-0001.

SPD.when: When you want to think through what a shopper is waiting for on a slow page before anyone changes code.
SPD.tune: Describe the slow moment in plain words, such as the main product image showing late on a phone, and bring any trace you have. Ask for one small change that can be undone, with a stop rule, not a promised score. Read SPD-0006 and SPD-0004.

CRO.when: When you have a test idea and need to know if your traffic and orders can prove it.
CRO.tune: Give it monthly orders, sessions and conversion rate for the page from Shopify and GA4. Under about 30 orders a month, do research instead of tests, and small stores should only test big changes. Read CRO-0011, CRO-0005 and CRO-0024.

CRO.when: When conversion is poor and you want proof of where and why before you test anything.
CRO.tune: Feed it GA4 funnel exports, Shopify sessions by device and the survey or recording tools you have. Check the purchase event first, since broken tracking sends the research the wrong way. Read CRO-0003, LPG-0040 and MEA-0002.

CRO.when: When you have heatmaps or session recordings and do not know what to look for.
CRO.tune: Export scroll maps, click maps and rage click rates from Microsoft Clarity or Hotjar for your top product and collection pages. Treat rage clicks under 1 to 2% of sessions as normal and look for sections that get many clicks but few viewers. Read CRO-0022, CRO-0023 and LPG-0051.

CRO.when: When shoppers visit your product page but few add to cart and you do not know why.
CRO.tune: Say what you sell and how many orders you get a day, then run the on-page survey on the product page with the biggest drop. Turn the top answers into test ideas, not instant fixes. Read LPG-0042 and CRO-0018.

CRO.when: When you want buyers to tell you what made them buy and what almost stopped them.
CRO.tune: Keep the thank-you page survey to two questions: what made you buy today, and what almost stopped you. Feed the near-miss answers into test ideas and page copy, and list AI assistants in the how-did-you-hear question. Read CRO-0018, LPG-0042 and AEO-0020.

CRO.when: When you have more test ideas than traffic and need to choose by evidence, not opinion.
CRO.tune: Paste each idea with the research behind it, plus traffic and gross profit per order. Rank by expected gross profit: chance of a win, likely lift, profit per order and traffic exposed, minus build cost. Read CRO-0013, CRO-0012 and CRO-0020.

CRO.when: When your store has modest traffic and small tests keep ending with no clear winner.
CRO.tune: Give it monthly sessions and orders and your top pages by revenue. Below about 300,000 sessions a month, test whole new pages, offers or product page redesigns rather than small tweaks. Read CRO-0019, CRO-0001 and CRO-0011.

CRO.when: When you want to run a test on Shopify and need to know what your plan and tools allow.
CRO.tune: Tell it your Shopify plan, theme and testing app. Stores not on Plus cannot test checkout with browser tools, flicker can inflate a variant's lift, and the same product should never be sold at two test prices. Read CRO-0016, CRO-0008 and CRO-0009.

CRO.when: When you want to test ads, audiences or landing pages through Meta's own experiment tools.
CRO.tune: Give it daily spend, cost per purchase and purchase volume from Ads Manager so the test is sized honestly. Use a Meta A/B test or a lift study instead of comparing two ad sets by eye. Read CRO-0005, CRO-0015 and MEA-0033.

CRO.when: When a test has ended and you need to know if the result is real before you roll it out.
CRO.tune: Give it visitors, orders and revenue for each version by day, plus the planned sample size and dates. Check for an uneven traffic split and early stopping, and judge on revenue or profit per visitor, not conversion rate alone. Read CRO-0007, CRO-0017 and CRO-0010.

CRO.when: When you tested offers or bundles and need to know which one earns more profit per visitor.
CRO.tune: Paste sessions, orders and revenue for each offer with unit cost, shipping and the cost of any gift or discount. A bigger pack or gift can lift revenue while cutting profit, and revenue per visitor needs far more traffic to read. Read CRO-0014 and MEA-0047.

CRO.when: When you test often and want one log that ranks ideas, runs one test at a time and reads each result.
CRO.tune: Give it your store numbers each month and every test's dates and results as they end. Expect most tests to lose, since a 30 to 35% win rate is very good. Read CRO-0020, CRO-0012 and CRO-0015.

CRO.when: When you shipped several test winners and total sales did not rise to match.
CRO.tune: Name the changes or channel you doubt and give it traffic and order counts. Hold a share of visitors back from all shipped winners for a few weeks to see what they really add together. Read CRO-0012 and MEA-0033.

CRO.when: When you want a second view on a page's message or a test plan, grounded in what buyers say.
CRO.tune: Bring the page, the survey answers and the test plan, and ask it to challenge the hypothesis before anything is built. Do not use it for exact statistics; pair it with the verdict check. Read CRO-0003 and LPG-0042.

CRO.when: When a test lift looks too good to be true and you need to explain the uncertainty in plain words.
CRO.tune: Give it the result ranges, sample sizes and the claim someone wants to make from the test. Ask it to say what the numbers do not show before anyone plans around the lift. Read CRO-0012, CRO-0006 and CRO-0017.

MCR.when: When you need next month's ad ideas to be truly different, not more versions of the one ad that already works.
MCR.tune: Feed it product reviews, post-purchase survey answers and your top ad names from a Meta export, and ask for each concept to differ in persona, angle or offer. The store trap is calling a new colour or pose a new concept; read MCR-0022 and MCR-0050 before choosing cells.

MCR.when: When you are setting next month's creative plan and need to know how many new ads to make.
MCR.tune: Give it monthly Meta spend, target cost per purchase and your hit rate from the last 60 to 90 days of ads, not a guess. Small stores often copy big-brand quotas they cannot produce, so check the spend bands in MCR-0058 and MCR-0082 first.

MCR.when: When results have gone flat across many ads and you think they might all be the same idea.
MCR.tune: Paste every live ad with its persona, angle, offer and format, plus cold frequency from the Meta export. Treat near copies as one ad, because Meta groups them; read MCR-0078 and MCR-0040 before you brief anything new.

MCR.when: When you want a full review of your Meta ads for tired creative, missing formats and ads that do not fit Reels, Stories or Feed.
MCR.tune: Run it on an ad-level Meta export with spend, frequency, click rate and purchases over at least 14 days, plus the ad files. Its benchmarks are generic, so judge fatigue against your own past winners and check MCR-0036 and MCR-0060 before adding formats for their own sake.

MCR.when: When you have a long list of video hooks and need to pick the few worth filming.
MCR.tune: Give it the hooks, the buyer each one targets and the 3-second view rate of past hooks if you have it. Score the spoken line, on-screen text and first shot separately, and drop hooks that stop the scroll but attract non-buyers (MCR-0026, MCR-0028).

MCR.when: When your founder is willing to film and you want a month or more of founder ads from one shoot.
MCR.tune: Feed it real reviews, the founder story and product proof, then let it build the hook-by-body grid before the shoot. Keep founder ads as one part of the mix, not the whole account, and start the script with a claim and its proof (MCR-0006, MCR-0008).

MCR.when: When you need a still image ad for Meta and want a proven pattern that fits cold or warm buyers.
MCR.tune: Give it the product page, review quotes and the buyer's awareness stage. Make each static either fully clear or a deliberate curiosity gap, and send curiosity statics to a page that teaches (MCR-0019, MCR-0024).

MCR.when: When you have a finished image ad and want a second opinion before you put money behind it.
MCR.tune: Attach the image and the exact product or collection page it sends people to. A clever headline with a page that does not explain it is the common store miss, so check MCR-0019 and MCR-0080 first.

MCR.when: When your best ad is losing spend or return and you want to bring it back before starting from zero.
MCR.tune: Give it the ad's weekly spend, return and frequency since launch from the Meta export, plus the script. Try new openers or a new setting with the same body before writing off the idea (MCR-0012, MCR-0047).

MCR.when: When one video ad is winning and you want versions of it for other kinds of buyers.
MCR.tune: Feed it the winning script, review quotes grouped by buyer type and the product's ingredients or features. Change only the persona and the matching proof, keep the structure, and give each version a page that matches (MCR-0073, MCR-0074).

MCR.when: When your product needs explaining and short ads are not turning into sales.
MCR.tune: Give it the mechanism, review quotes in customers' own words and every proof point you can back. Use a long video only when buyers do not understand the product yet, then test several hooks on one working body (MCR-0033, MCR-0031).

MCR.when: When you have a few ads that sell, yours or a rival's, and want to know what they share before you brief more.
MCR.tune: Paste ten or more winners with spend and how long each ran, tagged by segment, angle, hook and format. Swap one part at a time, and try your winning ideas in new formats before inventing new ideas (MCR-0051, MCR-0052).

MCR.when: When you want to see what rival stores are running on Meta and where they leave gaps.
MCR.tune: Pick rivals one or two sizes bigger than you, and study ads that have run longest rather than the newest ones. Never copy their words or images, and treat formats that every guru now teaches as past their peak (MCR-0034, MCR-0062).

MCR.when: When most of your spend sits on two or three ads and you want to spread the risk across sources and formats.
MCR.tune: Give it your live ads with spend, source (AI, creator, in-house), format and awareness stage. Aim for many distinct formats with spend spread across them, and split effort between remaking winners, fixing near misses and new bets (MCR-0036, MCR-0042).

MCR.when: When an ad is not reaching new people, or the picture and the words seem to speak to different buyers.
MCR.tune: Attach the ad image or script with its primary text and the page it sends to. Keep one ad on one awareness stage, and make sure most of your ads speak to people who do not know you yet (MCR-0056, MCR-0057).

ADC.when: When you are setting up Meta ads for your store, or you took over an account full of campaigns nobody can explain.
ADC.tune: Give it monthly spend, products with gross margin and the countries you sell to. Start from one cold campaign and add campaigns only for real business splits, grouped by concept rather than launch date (ADC-0030, ADC-0058).

ADC.when: When you are about to launch a batch of new ads and old winners keep taking all the budget.
ADC.tune: Give it your daily budget, target cost per purchase and the concepts in the batch. Put each batch of four to eight ads in its own named ad set with a small spend floor, and move unspent but worthy ads to a separate set (ADC-0016, ADC-0031).

ADC.when: When a test batch has run for a week or two and you need to know which ads to keep, leave or replace.
ADC.tune: Paste results by ad set and ad from the Meta export with spend, purchases and click rate. Judge a concept after about three times your target cost per purchase, at ad set level, and do not crown a high click-rate ad that sells nothing (ADC-0039, ADC-0059, MCR-0029).

ADC.when: When you do not know how much to spend on new ads before you judge them.
ADC.tune: Give it your target cost per purchase from your margin, the number of ads and how many days the test can run. At low daily budgets, cap impressions per ad so each one gets a fair look (ADC-0066, ADC-0004).

ADC.when: When you want to know whether your share of winning ads is normal and how many ads to make next.
ADC.tune: Paste a prospecting ad export covering at least two weeks and 20 or more ads. Count a winner only if it took a real share of spend at target cost, and expect a few ads to hold most spend under campaign budgets (ADC-0017, ADC-0014).

ADC.when: When some ads are winning and you want to spend more without losing money.
ADC.tune: Give it winning ads, product margins, cash on hand and 30 days of Shopify net sales next to Meta spend. Scale on the cost of the next customer, not the average, and judge on store cash over 30 days, not platform return (ADC-0049, ADC-0034).

ADC.when: When strong Meta returns might be coming from people who already buy from you anyway.
ADC.tune: Give it the size of your Shopify or Klaviyo customer list synced to Meta, recent CPM and current 30-day frequency on that audience. Set the spend in money from list size, CPM and a frequency cap, not as a share of budget (ADC-0021, ADC-0068).

ADC.when: When you want a full health check of your Meta ad account before you change anything or raise spend.
ADC.tune: Run it on Meta Ads Manager exports, Events Manager screenshots and your Shopify order count for the same dates. Fix data first, then structure, then creative, and be wary of advice to use flexible ads that hide which creative sold (ADC-0028, ADC-0065).

ADC.when: When Meta says your ads are doing great but your store sales do not agree.
ADC.tune: Give it the attribution setting on each campaign plus Meta's compare-attribution and incremental columns next to Shopify new-customer sales. Expect catalog and retargeting ads to shrink most on an incremental view, and expect the click-window gap to widen in November (ADC-0010, ADC-0046).

ADC.when: When you need to decide where Meta budget should move and which ad sets to cut or grow.
ADC.tune: Give it at least 14 days of campaign and ad set spend, results and bid settings. Its built-in rules include a 20 percent raise limit and a 70/20/10 split, so check ADC-0056 and ADC-0053 and let your own break-even numbers win.

ADC.when: When Meta keeps spending on people who already know you, or a new concept lost and you cannot tell why.
ADC.tune: Describe frequency, audience segment reports and what changed, with at least 7 days of data. Treat age, gender and interests as hints on broad targeting, and keep exclusions as the hard controls (ADC-0055, ADC-0029).

ADC.when: When you need campaign concepts and copy for each Meta placement written from your brand and audit notes.
ADC.tune: Give it a brand profile built from your store, the top review themes and any audit findings, and ask for primary text, headlines and calls to action per placement. Front-load the headline, since most people read nothing else, and name the buyer group in the copy (ADC-0018, ADC-0032).

ADC.when: When one ad works and you want more ads in the same voice for your best customer groups.
ADC.tune: Paste the winning ad and your top customer groups from surveys or Shopify tags. Put the target group's name in the copy instead of relying on interest targeting, and launch the variants as their own ad set (ADC-0032, ADC-0058).

ADC.when: When you are starting TikTok ads for your store and want setup, a first test and a clear read on it.
ADC.tune: Give it your pixel status, daily budget, target cost per purchase and three different styles of video. Use one broad audience rather than stacked interests, and size ad groups near twice your target cost (ADC-0035, ADC-0063).

ADC.when: When Black Friday or another big sale is coming and you need to know how many ads to have ready.
ADC.tune: Give it last year's top sale ads with their daily spend ceilings, this year's spend target and dates. Spread budget into September and October, keep evergreen campaigns running, and write scaling rules before the sale starts (ADC-0048, ADC-0050).

GAD.when: When you are about to run Google Ads for your store for the first time.
GAD.tune: Give it your catalogue size, monthly orders, budget and whether purchase tracking already works. Start on Search and Shopping with your bestsellers, and add Performance Max only once the account has steady conversions (GAD-0033, GAD-0030).

GAD.when: When Google shows more sales than your store does, or before you raise any Google budget.
GAD.tune: Paste the conversion actions list and a screenshot of one real Shopify test order as Google recorded it. GA4 imports set as the main purchase action are a common leak, and recent days always look weak, so check GAD-0042 and GAD-0035.

GAD.when: When you took over a Google Ads account, or Google results look fine but store growth does not match.
GAD.tune: Give it campaign, search term and Shopping exports plus Shopify sales for the same dates. Look first for brand traffic hiding inside Performance Max and Shopping, which makes cold returns look better than they are (GAD-0010, GAD-0028).

GAD.when: When products show as disapproved in Merchant Center, or before you put more money into Shopping.
GAD.tune: Paste the Merchant Center diagnostics export and a few live product page prices. Price mismatches between feed and page are a top cause, and selling in several currencies needs a feed for each (GAD-0005, GAD-0049).

GAD.when: When your Shopping ads get seen but few people click or buy.
GAD.tune: Give it the Shopify product export and the search terms report filtered to converting terms. Lead titles with what people search, such as product type, material and colour, and put the brand last unless people search for it (GAD-0009, GAD-0044).

GAD.when: When you are starting Google Shopping and want spend on the few products that already sell.
GAD.tune: Give it your top 5 to 10 products by Shopify sales with cost per purchase if you have it, plus your brand terms for negatives. Concentrate cold budget on the products that convert cheapest before widening (GAD-0030, GAD-0031).

GAD.when: When Performance Max or Shopping returns look strong but new customers are not growing.
GAD.tune: Give it campaign totals, the search terms report and your brand and product names. Keep brand in its own exact-match campaigns with exclusions everywhere else, and keep brand spend a small share of the total (GAD-0003, GAD-0024).

GAD.when: When you are not sure which bid strategy to use, or spend dropped after you raised a target.
GAD.tune: Give it 30 to 60 days of campaign conversions, value and current targets, plus break-even return from your margin. Set a new target below what the campaign already achieves and raise it in small steps, because a target set too high starves the campaign (GAD-0007, GAD-0053).

GAD.when: When Search and Shopping work and you are deciding whether to add Performance Max.
GAD.tune: Give it the catalogue, daily budget, monthly conversions and break-even return. Do not launch without a clean feed and working purchase tracking, split asset groups by product type, and leave a return target off at first (GAD-0026, GAD-0016).

GAD.when: When Performance Max is spending on YouTube or Gmail and you want it pulled back to Shopping.
GAD.tune: Give it your Shopping setup, product count and placement report. Remove asset groups, turn off automatic assets and URL expansion, and check placements whenever clicks jump while return falls (GAD-0048, GAD-0055).

GAD.when: When you want a weekly routine for Standard Shopping and need to know which products to cut, fix or fund.
GAD.tune: Paste a weekly product-level Shopping export with clicks, cost, conversions and value, plus current prices. A sudden drop in click rate on one product often means a rival cut its price, so check prices before blaming bids (GAD-0034, GAD-0019).

GAD.when: When your search terms report is full of searches you never meant to pay for.
GAD.tune: Paste 30 to 90 days of search terms from Shopping, Search and Performance Max with conversions. Promote proven terms into keywords and titles, and keep brand terms as negatives in every cold campaign (GAD-0044, GAD-0028).

GAD.when: When your product solves a problem people search for in plain words and Shopping already works.
GAD.tune: Give it the problem searches buyers type, an education or advertorial page and your proof. Write the ad to the problem, not the product name, and keep most Google spend in Shopping while you test this (GAD-0025, GAD-0054).

GAD.when: When Google revenue or return fell and you want to know why before you rebuild anything.
GAD.tune: Give it 90 days of weekly results, the change history and stock-outs from Shopify. Check feed disapprovals, stock-outs and raised targets first, and make targeted fixes, since a rebuild resets learning (GAD-0037, GAD-0036).

GAD.when: When you want to raise your Google budget and are not sure the account can take it.
GAD.tune: Give it budget use, return against target and back-end store revenue by campaign. Fix an unprofitable campaign at its current budget first, and judge scaling on store revenue, not platform return (GAD-0032, GAD-0045).

ORG.when: When you have posted for a few weeks and cannot tell which kind of post works.
ORG.tune: Give it at least 20 posts with views, shares, saves, comments and the share of views from non-followers. Judge by your goal, shares for growth and comments for buyers, and turn a format that wins again and again into a named series (ORG-0019, ORG-0011).

ORG.when: When your product videos get few views and you think the first three seconds are the problem.
ORG.tune: Give it the product, the post idea and the buyer it is for. Keep on-screen hook text short and simple, and make sure the first frame shows the product being used (ORG-0016, ORG-0017).

ORG.when: When you have a product and a phone and want a plan for what videos to film this week.
ORG.tune: Tell it who can go on camera, what the product does on screen and who buys it. Pick two or three expert formats or a numbered series that shows the product every time, and post many videos on one topic for one buyer (ORG-0015, ORG-0018, ORG-0023).

ORG.when: When your store's social posts get few views and you want to rule out setup problems first.
ORG.tune: List each account, its country settings and its last 20 posts with views. Creator-style accounts set up in the target country usually reach further than brand accounts, and one hero platform plus email beats spreading thin (ORG-0013, ORG-0022).

ORG.when: When one of your posts got far more views than usual and you want to run it as an ad.
ORG.tune: Give it 30 or more recent posts with views so it can find real outliers against your normal. Run a post that beat your usual views by a wide margin as-is first, and ignore high-view rival videos with low engagement, since those are often paid (ORG-0035, ORG-0010).

ORG.when: When your videos get views but few people reach your store or email list.
ORG.tune: Give it a free guide, size chart or quiz worth a comment, your DM tool and your Klaviyo list setup. Swap link-in-bio for a comment keyword, but keep calls to action off posts until they reach steady views (ORG-0021, ORG-0014).

ORG.when: When you want a steady supply of creator videos for ads without paying a studio.
ORG.tune: Give it product cost, shipping cost, margin and how many videos you need a month. Tier creators by job, a few for authority and many smaller ones for volume, and keep partner-ad terms in writing (ORG-0004, ORG-0009).

ORG.when: When a creator sends you a price and you cannot tell if it is fair.
ORG.tune: Give it your recent Meta CPM, the creator's last 10 video views and your product and postage cost. Price the post off your own paid reach, and offer a floor or a commission for shop sellers rather than a share of ad spend (ORG-0041, ORG-0036).

ORG.when: When you want to find creators yourself instead of paying an agency.
ORG.tune: Describe your buyer from reviews and order data, the platforms they use and the hours your team has. Scouts should match creators to the buyer, not to follower counts (ORG-0040, ORG-0004).

ORG.when: When you have long videos or lots of footage that could be cut into many short clips by other people.
ORG.tune: Give it your footage, a capped budget, a do-not-say list and who approves clips. Pay only for approved clips, re-post stories that already won in new formats, and get claims checked first (ORG-0037, ORG-0026).

ORG.when: When the founder wants to post regular videos and keeps running out of ideas.
ORG.tune: Feed it real buyer questions from support tickets, reviews and DMs. Keep most videos tightly on the exact buyer, give help without asking for the sale, and stick to one topic long enough for the platform to learn who to show it to (ORG-0001, ORG-0003, ORG-0023).

ORG.when: When you want to sell through live auctions or live shows and need a run order and a profit check.
ORG.tune: Give it your stock list with costs, show length and current follower count. Start with many short shows if you have no audience, promote big shows three times, and check giveaways and low opening bids against margin (ORG-0005, ORG-0006, ORG-0007, ORG-0008).

ORG.when: When a creator or athlete already uses your product daily and you are thinking about a long deal.
ORG.tune: Describe the person, how long they have used the product and your company's stage. Sign only people who already use it, think in multi-year terms, and take the outline to a lawyer and accountant (ORG-0039, ORG-0034).

ORG.when: When you want buyers or a launch waitlist to bring in new customers.
ORG.tune: Give it product margin, repeat rate and what you can give as a reward. For a launch, product rewards that grow with each referral can beat cash, so read ORG-0030 before choosing rewards.

ORG.when: When you want to rethink where your buyers really pay attention and what free help would earn it.
ORG.tune: Bring your last month of posts, the platforms your buyers use and what you sell. Use the lens to plan useful posts with no ask, and let paid ads carry the selling (ORG-0003, ORG-0022).

EML.when: When your email flows were set up a while ago and nobody has checked which ones are missing or firing on the wrong trigger.
EML.tune: Feed it a Klaviyo flow export (trigger, filters, delays, message count) plus last 90 days of flow revenue per recipient. The usual store trap is an 'abandoned cart' flow that really fires on Checkout Started, so check EML-0018 and EML-0019 first and compare delays to EML-0064.

EML.when: When people join your list through a pop-up but the welcome flow is still the default or earns little.
EML.tune: Give it the sign-up offer, top five sellers from a Shopify sales-by-product report, founder story and three real reviews. Read EML-0047 and EML-0058 before picking the offer size, and keep the first 72 hours dense as in EML-0060.

EML.when: When your cart emails give away a code in the first message or only start once checkout begins.
EML.tune: Bring gross margin per order, shipping and returns terms and current flow timing from Klaviyo. Build a separate Added to Cart flow (EML-0018), hold any discount until late in the flow (EML-0044), and if you also text, send email and SMS together as in EML-0012.

EML.when: When past buyers have gone quiet and your win-back still fires at the tool's default 90 days.
EML.tune: Pull days between first and second order from a Shopify order export so the trigger matches your real reorder gap, not a template. Screen out buyers with a return or complaint first (EML-0050), and for subscriptions time the offer as in EML-0006.

EML.when: When your product gets used up and most buyers still order only once.
EML.tune: Give it how many days one unit lasts per product and real delivery times, then time reminders near 75 percent of use (EML-0049). Most second orders land inside 30 days (EML-0062), so check the stage split in EML-0053 before adding offers.

EML.when: When first-time and repeat buyers get the same flow emails and the same discounts.
EML.tune: Give it your flow list and how you define new, returning and loyal from Shopify order counts. Split at the top of each flow (EML-0053) and keep active subscribers out of sale sends (EML-0001).

EML.when: When your pop-up signs up only a small share of visitors and you do not know what to change first.
EML.tune: Give it current pop-up sign-up rate, average order value and margin. Ask for the phone on step two with the same offer (EML-0038), and check the offer against your subscription offer so the pop-up does not undercut it (OFF-0037).

EML.when: When you send every campaign to your whole list and your open rate keeps sliding.
EML.tune: Give it list size, send pace and the Klaviyo fields you have for opens, clicks, site visits and orders. Define engaged without Apple privacy opens (EML-0011) and set a clear unengaged rule (EML-0042) before any suppression.

EML.when: When you have just set up or switched your email tool, or email revenue looks too good to be true.
EML.tune: Paste SPF, DKIM and DMARC records plus Klaviyo smart sending and attribution settings. Check the attribution window against EML-0013 and EML-0056 before trusting any flow revenue number.

EML.when: When opens have dropped for weeks and your emails seem to be landing in spam or promotions.
EML.tune: Bring 60 days of campaign results by segment and spam complaint counts from Klaviyo. Follow the narrow-then-widen pacing in EML-0021, judge recovery against EML-0059, and clean out only after the consent check.

EML.when: When you only email around sales and want a steady plan for the month.
EML.tune: Give it monthly revenue, list size, launch and restock dates and who writes each send. Set the pace from EML-0041 and the content mix from EML-0016, and plan one owned moment per quarter (EML-0055).

EML.when: When you need to decide which launches and sales deserve a text this month and how often to send.
EML.tune: Give it SMS list size, cost per text and last month's SMS click and unsubscribe rates. Start from about one campaign a week (EML-0025, EML-0039) and let a holdout settle frequency as in EML-0036.

EML.when: When a text is written and you want its cost and rule problems checked before it goes to the whole list.
EML.tune: Paste the exact text, list size and send time. Watch for one extra character or an emoji doubling the billed parts (EML-0024), and use images only where EML-0028 says they pay.

EML.when: When the month ends and you want to know what your email and texts really earned and what broke.
EML.tune: Feed Klaviyo campaign and flow exports, Shopify orders for the same dates and list growth. Read revenue per recipient by cohort (EML-0057) rather than attributed share, which EML-0056 warns mostly measures opens.

EML.when: When your buyers, often in India, already chat on WhatsApp and you want to sell and answer questions there.
EML.tune: Give it opt-in counts, order volume and your top support questions. Lean on automated journeys over broadcasts (EML-0048), and only message people who opted in, since the number can be banned.

SEO.when: When you are deciding whether search is worth your time or an agency's fee for your store.
SEO.tune: Give it margin per order, order value, monthly hours and cash, and a few target terms with search volume. Search takes months, so if you need sales this quarter expect a not-now answer. Read SEO-0008 and SEO-0013.

SEO.when: When you have a few hours a month for search and want one routine you can repeat.
SEO.tune: Give it your platform, catalogue size and Search Console access. Put collection pages before blog posts, since they carry most organic revenue on stores with many products. Read SEO-0001 and SEO-0003.

SEO.when: When you have a pile of keyword ideas and need to know which ones deserve a page.
SEO.tune: Paste keyword exports from Google Keyword Planner, Ahrefs or Semrush with volume and difficulty, plus your product list. Keep terms with buying intent and difficulty a small store can win, and drop terms for things you do not sell. Read SEO-0008.

SEO.when: When you need each page to target its own search term so your pages stop competing.
SEO.tune: Give it your catalogue, current page addresses and the checked keyword list. Map one topic to one page and mark each as a collection, product or blog page. Read SEO-0012, SEO-0003 and SEO-0011.

SEO.when: When you sell a range but have only a few broad collections and want more ways to be found.
SEO.tune: Give it your product export with tags and attributes plus keyword data. Build a sub-collection for each searched variant, such as a style or a price band, each aimed at one search. Read SEO-0012, SEO-0001 and SEO-0003.

SEO.when: When you are launching a collection, or one ranks poorly with only a name and a product grid.
SEO.tune: Give it the collection, its target keyword and the pages that rank for it now. Put the keyword first in the title and alone in the H1, and show 36 to 48 products per page. Read SEO-0005.

SEO.when: When you are writing or fixing a product page for a product people search for by name.
SEO.tune: Give it supplier specs, your own product facts, reviews and the target term. Put specifications in a table and keep the page live with a back-in-stock note when it sells out. Read SEO-0007 and AEO-0031.

SEO.when: When Search Console shows many duplicate or crawled but not indexed pages on your Shopify store.
SEO.tune: Give it a duplicate of your theme and a crawl or Search Console page indexing export. Make product grid links point to plain product addresses, then rebuild breadcrumbs so they do not depend on the old path. Read SEO-0004.

SEO.when: When a site audit gives you hundreds of warnings and you need the few that matter for sales.
SEO.tune: Paste a crawler export and Search Console page indexing data. Rank fixes on the collection and product pages that earn money first, and ignore warnings on pages nobody visits. Read SEO-0003 and SEO-0013.

SEO.when: When you want a 90-day search plan for one product category instead of spreading effort thin.
SEO.tune: Pick your best-margin category and give it the main rivals and the questions buyers ask. Start with the most-aware searches, such as one brand versus another and alternatives, and cover Google and AI answers together. Read SEO-0009, SEO-0010 and AEO-0024.

SEO.when: When shoppers search for your rivals by name and you want comparison pages built in the right order.
SEO.tune: Give it your top rivals, Search Console queries that name them and honest product facts. Stick to the formats that tend to pay: you versus a rival, alternatives, best for a use, and buying guides. Read SEO-0011 and AEO-0006.

SEO.when: When your collections sit just off page one and rivals have many more sites linking to them.
SEO.tune: Give it your linking domains and those of three rivals from Ahrefs or Semrush. Size the gap against the rival average, point early links at the home page and top collections, and avoid paid links. Read SEO-0006 and SEO-0002.

SEO.when: When you have a few months of Search Console data and want to know what to work on this month.
SEO.tune: Export queries and pages for the last three months. Push pages that rank just off page one with many views, and turn real queries into FAQ answers. Read SEO-0013 and AEO-0005.

SEO.when: When organic clicks fell and you need to know which pages lost them and why.
SEO.tune: Export Search Console by page and query for the drop period and the period before. If the position held but clicks fell, look for an AI answer above you before you change the page. Read AEO-0005 and AEO-0019.

SEO.when: When an SEO or AI search agency sends you a proposal and you are about to sign.
SEO.tune: Paste the proposal, sample reports and any promises about links or page counts. Flag paid link schemes and plans to publish hundreds of AI-written pages, which often rise and then crash. Read SEO-0002, AEO-0018 and AEO-0033.

AEO.when: When you want one run from shopper questions to a list of who AI names today and the page fixes that close the gap.
AEO.tune: Give it your products, rivals and real customer questions from email, chat and reviews. Save the first run as a baseline so you can rerun the same questions later. Read AEO-0001, AEO-0012 and AEO-0035.

AEO.when: When you want to know if AI search bots can reach and read your product pages before any other AI work.
AEO.tune: Give it your robots.txt, your CDN bot settings and a few product page links. Reload key pages with JavaScript turned off to check that reviews and FAQs still show. Read AEO-0028, AEO-0002 and AEO-0008.

AEO.when: When you need a robots.txt for AI bots and an llms.txt file written for your store.
AEO.tune: Paste your current robots.txt and sitemap address. Allow the AI search crawlers you want, keep cart and account pages blocked, and have a developer apply the files. Read AEO-0028 and AEO-0008.

AEO.when: When you run a Shopify store and want your catalogue data ready for AI shopping tools.
AEO.tune: Give it read access to the Shopify admin so it can check product data, categories and descriptions. AI shopping tools read the back-end catalogue, so fill product category, specs and variants in the admin, not only on the page. Read AEO-0003.

AEO.when: When you need the long, specific questions shoppers ask AI about products like yours.
AEO.tune: Feed it support emails, chat logs, review questions and return reasons. Use the follow-up search wording in page titles, H1s and first sentences, and answer fit and compatibility questions in full. Read AEO-0016 and AEO-0031.
